Business Economics with Dr Karmini Sharma, Lectures 1 to 6

The whole course is one story.

How does a firm decide what to charge and how much to make, and when is the result good for everyone? Each lecture adds one piece. Work through the lectures, apply them with the playbook, and drill until the problem sets feel routine.

Your progress

Progress is kept in this browser. Sign in to keep it across devices.

How the problem sets test you: Part A is 10–16 multiple-choice questions where every wrong option is a planted mistake (forgot α, read the price off MR, counted a sunk cost, added a negative quantity). Part B turns calculations into a decision plus a 150-word memo and asks you to draw labelled diagrams. The playbook is organised around exactly those moves.
L1ConsumersPeople maximise utility on a budget, which gives a demand function. L2DemandAdd people up to get market demand. Elasticity decides revenue. L3CostsProduction gives costs. MC cuts AC at its minimum. L4SupplyPrice takers set P = MC, which gives supply. Supply meets demand. L5CompetitionFree entry pushes P to min ATC. Caps and taxes create deadweight loss. L6MonopolyNo entry, so MR < P. The firm sells less, charges more, and a DWL appears.
The spine you need to be able to say out loud:
Preferences + budget → demand \(x_1^*=\alpha M/p_1\) → add people up → market demand → its sensitivity is elasticity, which decides whether a price rise raises revenue: \(\frac{dTR}{dp}=D(1-\varepsilon)\).
Inputs + technology → production → priced inputs give costs → \(MC=w/MP\) → a price taker sets P = MC → that is its supply curve → add firms → market supply → meets demand at equilibrium.
With free entry, profit attracts rivals until P = min ATC, giving the efficient quantity and no deadweight loss. Block entry (monopoly) and the firm sets MR = MC with MR < P, so price rises, output falls, and a deadweight loss appears. The markup is set by elasticity: \(\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac1e\).

The recurring cast (the lecturer reuses them, so you should too)

☕ The coffee drinker (L1–2)

\(\alpha=0.3,\ M=£30\), so \(x_1=9/p_1\): 9, 4.5, 3 and 1.8 cups at £1, £2, £3 and £5.

☂ Priya's BrollyGo (L1–3)

£2 per unlock. Rain shifts demand. Costs are \(TC=5{,}000+0.40Q\): a big fixed cost, so average cost keeps falling.

🍕 The pizza stall (L2)

\(Q=25-5P\). Revenue peaks at £2.50, where \(\varepsilon=1\). Elasticity is \(5P/Q\).

📦 The delivery firm (L3)

One depot (£50/day), workers at £30. MP peaks at 60 with the 4th worker. \(MC=30/MP\).

☕ Sam's café (L4–6)

One of 20 cafés at £3, selling 150 cups at the lowest ATC. Shutdown at £1.50, break-even at £3. Becomes a monopoly kiosk in L6: \(P=6-Q\).

🚇 The transport network (L6)

Fixed cost £1,250/day, MC = £1. A natural monopoly: should the regulator set P = MC or P = AC?
Lecture 1 · Introduction & consumer theory

You already know this maths. The constraints are just made of money.

A consumer picks the best bundle she can afford. Solving that one optimisation gives the demand function, and the rest of the course is built on it.
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS1 Q1–4, Q11)
R1 Optimal bundle via MRS = p₁/p₂R2 Elasticities by logsR4 Movement or shift
Hook
American Airlines' yield-management system (DINAMO) used demand forecasting, dynamic pricing and overbooking to earn an extra $1.4bn over three years, about the airline's entire profit margin at the time. It is the same constrained optimisation you already do in engineering, applied to a firm's own prices.
The engineer's translation
You solve "maximise output subject to constraints" all the time. Economics adds two twists. (1) The constraints are budgets, prices and other people, not materials and heat. (2) Every part of the system (customers, rivals, workers) is itself an optimiser with its own objective.

1. What economics is (and isn't) good at

Definition

Robbins (1932): the study of behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Course version: a quantitative social science that models rational agents and estimates causal effects.

Positive statements ✓

Testable predictions: "if coffee gets dearer, people buy less coffee." Economics is strong here.

Normative statements !

Value judgements: "we should raise the price." Economics only clarifies the menu of options. The final choice depends on priorities.

Non-strategic decisions

Your choice doesn't affect anyone else's: apples or oranges. (L1–L6)

Strategic decisions

Your choice changes rivals' choices and vice versa, like a duopolist's ad campaign. That's game theory, coming in L7.

Models are maps

"All models are wrong, but some are useful" (Box). A model states its assumptions and lets you change one thing ceteris paribus, which is the lab experiment economists can't usually run.

2. Three pricing stories you'll keep seeing

Coupons & discount codes

Price discrimination by self-selection. The hassle is the point: it filters customers. Price-sensitive bargain hunters bother with SAVE20 and pay £80. Busy customers don't, and pay £100. "The inconvenience is a filter, not a bug."

Airline revenue management

An empty seat earns nothing, and a seat sold too cheap too early loses money. The answer: forecast demand by fare class and days to departure, use dynamic pricing (cheap seats early, prices rising as the plane fills), and overbook using no-show probabilities.

Apple's versioning

Different models and storage sizes separate buyers. Find where demand is inelastic (loyal, will pay a premium) and price higher there. This is elasticity again, from Lecture 2.

3. The consumer's problem

Preferences → utility

Preferences rank bundles (more is better). A utility function \(u(x_1,x_2)\) represents that ranking. It is ordinal: \(u=10\) means only "better than \(u=9\)".
\[u(x_1,x_2)=x_1^{\alpha}\,x_2^{1-\alpha},\qquad 0<\alpha<1\]
More is always better (positive marginal utility), but each extra unit adds less (diminishing marginal utility): cups of water add 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.

The budget constraint

Every £ on good 1 is a £ you can't spend on good 2. You spend it all.
\[p_1x_1+p_2x_2=M\]
With \(M=£20,\ p_1=£4,\ p_2=£2\): one more coffee always costs \(p_1/p_2=2\) teas. That's the trade-off.
Derivation: from utility to demand in six lines (cover this and redo it yourself)
\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{1. Budget binds:} && p_1x_1+p_2x_2=M\\ &\text{2. Solve for } x_2: && x_2=\frac{M-p_1x_1}{p_2}\\ &\text{3. Substitute:} && u(x_1)=x_1^{\alpha}\left(\frac{M-p_1x_1}{p_2}\right)^{1-\alpha}\\ &\text{4. Differentiate, set to 0:} && \alpha x_1^{\alpha-1}B^{1-\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,p_1\,x_1^{\alpha}B^{-\alpha},\quad B\equiv M-p_1x_1\\ &\text{5. Cancel } x_1^{\alpha-1}B^{-\alpha}: && \alpha(M-p_1x_1)=(1-\alpha)p_1x_1\ \Rightarrow\ \alpha M=p_1x_1\\ &\text{6. Demand functions:} && \boxed{x_1^*=\frac{\alpha M}{p_1}},\qquad \boxed{x_2^*=\frac{(1-\alpha)M}{p_2}} \end{aligned}\]

Faster route, the engineer's trick: maximise \(\ln u=\alpha\ln x_1+(1-\alpha)\ln x_2\) instead (a monotonic transform keeps the same optimum). Then \(\frac{\alpha}{x_1}=\lambda p_1\) and \(\frac{1-\alpha}{x_2}=\lambda p_2\). Adding \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2=M\) gives \(\lambda=1/M\) at once.

The tangency condition (PS1 Q11(a) asks for this, not the substitution route)

At the optimum \(\dfrac{MU_1}{MU_2}=\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}\). The left side is the rate at which you're willing to give up good 2 for good 1 (the MRS). The right side is the rate at which the market makes you. If MRS > \(p_1/p_2\), moving £1 from good 2 to good 1 raises utility, so you keep moving until they're equal. For \(u=x_1^{a}x_2^{b}\) with \(a+b\neq1\), the budget shares are \(\frac{a}{a+b}\) and \(\frac{b}{a+b}\). Recipe R1 →
The insight hidden in that box: \(p_1x_1^*=\alpha M\). Spending on coffee is a fixed share \(\alpha\) of income, whatever the price. So a 10% price rise causes a 10% fall in quantity, and the own-price elasticity is exactly 1 (Lecture 2). Coffee is a normal good because \(x_1^*\) rises with \(M\).
Live model 1: the Cobb-Douglas consumerMove the sliders and watch how the budget line, the optimum and the demand curve respond.
Rationality caveat: real people pay for gyms they never use and keep forgotten free trials. The rational model is the baseline. Test it against data and amend it where behaviour systematically departs from it (behavioural economics).

Lecture 2 · Demand, elasticity, surplus

One number decides whether a price rise makes you richer.

Elasticity \(\varepsilon\) measures how hard customers push back on price. If \(\varepsilon<1\), a price rise raises revenue. If \(\varepsilon>1\), it lowers it. Revenue peaks at \(\varepsilon=1\).
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS1 Q2–13)
R3 Adding demand, kinksR4 Movement or shiftR5 Computing ε, validityR6 Revenue: exact vs approxR7 Consumer surplusR8 Price discrimination + arbitrage
Hook: Netflix, July 2011
Netflix raised the price of its DVD + streaming plan by 60% ($9.99 → $15.98) and lost about 800k US subscribers, ~3%. Implied short-run elasticity: \(3\%/60\%\approx 0.05\). Revenue rose about 49% year-on-year. Then churn jumped from 4.2% to 6.3%, the CEO wrote "I messed up", and the shares fell by roughly three-quarters. The lesson: an elasticity describes one horizon. Long-run elasticity is bigger.

1. Movement vs shift (the most-tested distinction in the course)

Price on the vertical axis

We draw the inverse demand curve: \(x_1=9/p_1 \iff p_1=9/x_1\). Read across from a price to get a quantity, or up from a quantity to get a willingness to pay.

Own price changes → MOVE ALONG

Café cuts £3 → £2: 3 → 4.5 cups. The curve itself doesn't move. Only the quantity demanded changes.

Anything else → SHIFT

Income (M £30 → £45: +2.25 cups at £2), tastes (\(\alpha\)), the price of a substitute or complement, health news, the weather (BrollyGo!). This changes demand.

2. Market demand: add HORIZONTALLY, watch for kinks

The method

(1) Find each person's choke price (where \(x=0\)). (2) Sort them and add the quantities of whoever is still buying. (3) Check that the pieces join at each kink.
\[x_A=12-p,\quad x_B=8-\tfrac p2\ \Rightarrow\ Q(p)=\begin{cases}20-1.5p & 0\le p\le 12\\ 8-0.5p & 1216\end{cases}\]
Problem set: add consumer C, \(x_C=5-p/4\) (try first) Choke prices are 12, 16 and 20. \[Q=\begin{cases}25-1.75p & p\le12\\13-0.75p & 1220\end{cases}\] Kinks join: at \(p=12\), \(25-21=13-9=4\) ✓, and at \(p=16\), \(13-12=5-4=1\) ✓.
\(Q=6\) is on the first piece: \(p=19/1.75\approx10.86\).
At \(p=10\): \(Q=7.5\), so \(\varepsilon=1.75\times10/7.5\approx2.33>1\), which is elastic.

3. A price change does two things at once

Substitution effect (always pulls toward the cheaper good)

Holding satisfaction fixed, coffee is now relatively cheaper, so you switch towards it. For a price fall this always raises quantity.

Income effect (sign depends on the good)

You're effectively richer. For a normal good it reinforces the substitution effect. For an inferior good it pushes the other way.
Price fallsSubstitutionIncomeTotalVerdict
Normal (coffee)+3+1.5+4.5Both effects agree: demand slopes down
Inferior (instant noodles)+3−1+2Still up, but the income effect pulls back
Giffen (rare, extreme)+1−3−2Demand slopes UP: the income effect wins

4. Elasticity: the dimensionless gain

Why not just use the slope?

Slopes depend on units (pence or pounds, cups or litres). Percentages don't, so you can compare coffee with cars. To an engineer, \(\varepsilon\) is a normalised gain.
\[\varepsilon=\frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta p}=\frac{\Delta Q/Q}{\Delta p/p}\ \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\to0\ }\ \varepsilon=-\frac{dQ}{dp}\cdot\frac{p}{Q}\]
Report it as a positive size.

Two shapes to know cold

Linear \(x=a-bp\): \(\varepsilon=\dfrac{bp}{a-bp}\). It is 0 at \(p=0\), 1 at \(p=\frac{a}{2b}\), and \(\to\infty\) at the choke price. Same slope, different \(\varepsilon\) all along the line.

Power law \(x=Ap^{-k}\): \(\varepsilon=k\) at every price. Cobb-Douglas is \(k=1\).
Arc-elasticity trap: with \(x=9/p\), going £2 → £3 gives \(\frac{-33\%}{+50\%}=0.67\), but £3 → £2 gives \(\frac{+50\%}{-33\%}=1.5\). The base changes with direction. That's why we use the point formula \(-\frac{dQ}{dp}\frac pQ\), which gives exactly 1 here.

What makes demand elastic?

Close substitutes · a long time horizon · a big budget share · a narrow market definition (food → fast food → McDonald's → Big Mac gets more elastic at each step).

UK estimates (Begg & Ward)

Spirits 1.3 · wine 1.2 · cereals 1.0 · fruit juice 0.8 · beer 0.5 · bread 0.0. A 10% price rise changes revenue by \(1.10(1-0.10\varepsilon)-1\): spirits −4.3%, bread +10%.

Reading \(\varepsilon=0.2\)

1% dearer → 0.2% fewer. A 10% rise gives revenue \(1.10\times0.98=1.078\), so +7.8%. A 10% cut gives \(0.90\times1.02=0.918\), so −8.2%.

5. Cross-price and income elasticity

Cross-price \(\varepsilon_X=\frac{dD_A}{dp_B}\frac{p_B}{D_A}\)

\(\varepsilon_X>0\): substitutes. Tea 10% dearer → coffee +4%, so \(\varepsilon_X=+0.4\).
\(\varepsilon_X<0\): complements. Ink 20% dearer → printers −6%, so \(\varepsilon_X=-0.3\).
\(\varepsilon_X\approx0\): unrelated (running shoes and bananas).

Income \(\varepsilon_M=\frac{dD}{dM}\frac{M}{D}\)

\(\varepsilon_M<0\): inferior (bus travel, instant noodles).
\(0<\varepsilon_M<1\): necessity, stable over the cycle.
\(\varepsilon_M>1\): luxury, whose budget share rises with income. If income falls 5%, a luxury with \(\varepsilon_M=2\) loses ~10% of sales.

6. The revenue rule, derived

\[TR(p)=p\,D(p)\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dTR}{dp}=D+pD'(p)=D\left[1+\frac{pD'(p)}{D}\right]=\boxed{D(p)\,(1-\varepsilon)}\]

\(\varepsilon>1\) (elastic)

Raise price → revenue falls. Cut price → revenue rises. The pizza stall at £4 → £3 gains 5 new units × £3 = £15 and loses 5 old units × £1 = £5, a net +£10k.

\(\varepsilon=1\) (unit)

Revenue is at its peak. For \(Q=25-5P\): \(P=£2.50,\ Q=12.5\), \(TR=£31.25\)k/day.

\(\varepsilon<1\) (inelastic)

Raise price → revenue rises. Tobacco (\(\varepsilon\approx0.4\)): +10% price ≈ +5.6% revenue. Business-class fares stay high, while leisure fares get cut.
Live model 2: the pizza stall, \(Q=25-5P\)Slide the price and watch \(\varepsilon\), revenue and consumer surplus.
consumer surplusrevenue \(P\times Q\)

7. Consumer surplus & price discrimination

The demand curve is a willingness-to-pay ranking

CS = WTP − price, summed over buyers: the triangle under demand and above the price.
\[CS=\tfrac12\,Q\,(P_{\max}-P)\qquad\text{pizza at £3: }\tfrac12\times10{,}000\times£2=£10{,}000\text{/day}\]

Price discrimination tries to capture CS

1st degree: each buyer pays their own max (haggling, personalised pricing). It is rarely perfect.
2nd degree: one menu for everyone, where the price depends on how much you buy (bulk tiers, popcorn combos).
3rd degree: the price depends on your group (students, off-peak, flexible tickets).
The rule: charge more to inelastic groups and less to elastic ones.

Lecture 3 · Firms and costs

The only costs that matter are the ones you can still change.

Costs come from production. Marginal cost mirrors marginal product, \(MC=w/MP\), and MC cuts every average cost at its minimum. In the long run every input can change, so \(LTC\le STC\).
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS2 Q1–6, Q18(a))
R9 Opportunity & sunkR10 MC from a tableR11 Min AVC / ATCR12 Cheapest input mixR13 Returns to scale
Hook: Concorde
Development costs ran far over estimate, yet Britain and France kept funding it because "stopping would waste what's been spent". That is the sunk cost fallacy. The only question is whether the money still to come buys benefits still to come. Good firms fail fast: set the budget and checkpoint in advance.
Hook: why do firms exist at all?
Using the market isn't free: searching, negotiating, contracting and checking are transaction costs. A firm does a task in-house when buying it costs more than managing it. That happens when the task is frequent, specific to the firm, or hard to write into a contract.

1. Production: one fixed depot, more and more workers

LTPMPAPMC = 30/MP
1404040.0£0.75
2905045.0£0.60
31455548.3£0.55
42056051.3£0.50
52555051.0£0.60
62954049.2£0.75
73253046.4£1.00
83452043.1£1.50
93551039.4£3.00
10360536.0£6.00

Why MP rises, then falls

Rising (workers 1–4): specialisation and learning by doing (one loads, one drives). Falling (5+): the depot and vans are fixed, so each new worker gets less space and fewer vans. That's the law of diminishing returns, which applies only when other inputs are fixed.

In algebra: \(Y=\sqrt{KL}\)

\(MPL=\tfrac12\sqrt{K/L}\), which falls as \(L\) rises (diminishing returns). More capital raises \(MPL\): workers with more machines add more at the margin.

The same "marginal vs average" rule everywhere

MP cuts AP at AP's peak. MC cuts AC at AC's minimum. Your grade average works the same way: a day-5 score above the average pulls it up.

2. Which costs count?

Opportunity cost

The value of the best alternative given up. Priya's own pressure washer: the accountant says £0, the economist says £50/day (the rent she gives up). Owning and renting cost the same.

The price of capital \(r\)

A £24k van resold for £16k after 2 years: depreciation £4k/yr plus forgone 5% interest £1.2k/yr gives £5,200/yr (£100/week), whatever the cash flows say.

Fixed · variable · sunk

Fixed: doesn't vary with output but is avoidable at renewal (rack leases). Variable: grows with output (cleaning each umbrella). Sunk: gone forever (the £40k app, the bolted-on branding). Sunk costs never affect a decision.

In the long run every cost is variable except sunk ones. A £100 refit is sunk. £10/month rent is fixed. An office you own has a fixed cost equal to the rent you forgo.

3. Short-run cost curves

\[TC=FC+VC,\quad AFC=\frac{FC}q,\quad AVC=\frac{VC}q,\quad ATC=AFC+AVC,\quad MC=\frac{dTC}{dq}=\frac{w}{MP}\]

Average ≠ marginal (the overtime trap)

The first 80 units cost £38 each and 20 overtime units cost £58, so AC = £4,200/100 = £42. The 101st unit sells for £50. Make it? No. It costs £58 (MC), so you lose £8. Compare price with MC, never with AC.
Worked: \(TC=100+15q-6q^2+q^3\), find every curve and both minima \(FC=100,\ VC=15q-6q^2+q^3\)
\(AVC=15-6q+q^2,\quad ATC=\frac{100}q+15-6q+q^2,\quad MC=15-12q+3q^2\)
Min AVC: \(\frac{d\,AVC}{dq}=-6+2q=0\Rightarrow q=3,\ AVC=6\). Check: \(MC(3)=15-36+27=6\) ✓
Min ATC: set \(MC=ATC\Rightarrow 2q^3-6q^2-100=0\Rightarrow q=5\), so \(ATC(5)=30=MC(5)\) ✓
ATC bottoms out later than AVC because AFC is still falling.
Live model 3: \(TC=F+s(15q-6q^2+q^3)\)Raise the fixed cost and see which curves move and which stay put.
MCAVCATCAFC

☂ BrollyGo's cost structure: \(TC=5{,}000+0.40Q\)

\(AC=5000/Q+0.40\): £5.40 at 1,000 unlocks, £2.90 at 2,000, £2.00 at 3,125 (break-even at the £2 price), and £0.90 at 10,000. MC stays at 40p while AC falls towards it. That is the signature of a big-fixed-cost business, and it reappears as natural monopoly in L6.

4. The long run: choose the mix, then the scale

The cost-minimising rule

Spend the next £ wherever it buys the most output, until both inputs give the same output per £:
\[\frac{MPL}{w}=\frac{MPK}{r}\iff \underbrace{\frac{MPL}{MPK}}_{MRTS}=\frac wr\]
With \(w=16,\ r=4\): bundle A (L = 25, K = 400) has \(MPL/w=0.125>MPK/r=0.031\), so shift spending to labour. Bundle B (50, 200) has both at 0.0625 and is optimal at £1,600.

Substitution = automation

For 100 parcels with a van at £50: at \(w=£30\), option B (5 workers, 2 vans) is cheapest at £250. At \(w=£60\), option C (3 workers, 4 vans) wins at £380. When an input gets dearer, the firm substitutes away from it.

For \(y=\sqrt{KL}\): \(L^*=\sqrt{r/w}\,y,\ K^*=\sqrt{w/r}\,y,\ LTC=2\sqrt{rw}\,y\). With \(w=16,\ r=4\) that's \(16y\). In the short run with \(K=200\), \(STC=800+0.08y^2\), which equals LTC only at \(y=100\).

Returns to scale

\(F(aK,aL)\ \gtrless\ aF(K,L)\). For \(K^\alpha L^\beta\), add the exponents: \(\alpha+\beta>1\) increasing, \(=1\) constant, \(<1\) decreasing. \(K^{0.6}L^{0.6}\): double the inputs → 2.30× output.

LATC = lower envelope of the SATCs

It is U-shaped for a different reason than SATC. SATC is U-shaped because of diminishing returns. LATC is U-shaped because of returns to scale. The bottom of LATC is the minimum efficient scale (MES).

Sources of (dis)economies

Economies: indivisible fixed costs (software), bulk buying, specialisation, the cube-square law (ships), learning. Diseconomies: management layers, duplication, slow communication, using up the best sites.

Case: Sainsbury's–Asda (blocked by the CMA, 25 April 2019)

They promised ~£1bn a year in lower prices from buying power (a bulk-buying economy of scale). The CMA found a substantial lessening of competition. Lower costs help buyers only if competition passes them on. Size can cut costs and weaken competition at the same time.

Lecture 4 · Profit, supply and equilibrium

Why does every café on the street charge £3?

A price taker sells until P = MC. Its supply curve is its MC curve, above min AVC in the short run and above min ATC in the long run. Add the firms up, cross with demand, and you get the price.
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS2 Q7–17, Q18)
R14 Economic profitR15 P = MC, profitR16 Shutdown & avoidable costsR3 Adding supplyR17 Equilibrium & combined shifts
Hook: Uber's surge, switched off
After a sold-out Madison Square Garden concert, surge pricing pulled more drivers in and waits stayed around 2.6 minutes. On one New Year's Eve a glitch switched surge off: waits rose to about 8 minutes and roughly a quarter of requests went unfilled. Supply slopes up, because each driver is a tiny firm moving up their MC curve.
Hook: closed on Mondays
Restaurants close on quiet Mondays, and airlines parked their planes in 2020. Rent and aircraft leases are due either way, so open only if revenue covers the costs you can avoid by closing: \(P\ge AVC\).

1. Economic profit ≠ accounting profit

Sam's revenue£24,000
− rent, beans, milk, wages, lease£20,000
= accounting profit£4,000
− what Sam could earn managing a chain's branch (opportunity cost = normal profit)£3,500
= economic (supernormal) profit£500

Zero economic profit is not zero income. It means you earn exactly your best alternative, which is why you stay.

2. The rule: MR = MC (and for a price taker MR = P)

The logic

One more cup adds MR to revenue and MC to cost. Keep selling while MR > MC. A price taker's demand is flat at the market price, so every cup adds exactly £3: \(MR=P\).
\[\Pi(q)=Pq-TC(q),\quad \frac{d\Pi}{dq}=P-MC(q)=0\ \Rightarrow\ P=MC,\quad \frac{d^2\Pi}{dq^2}=-MC'(q)<0\]
The second-order condition says MC must be rising where you stop.
Worked: \(TC=225+0.01q^2\) \(MC=0.02q=P\Rightarrow q=50P\), which is an upward-sloping supply curve.
\(P=£3\): \(q=150\), \(\Pi=450-(225+225)=£0\) (normal profit).
\(P=£4\): \(q=200\), \(\Pi=800-(225+400)=£175\).

3. Stay open or close? Two key prices

Live model 4: Sam's café decisionSimplified curves with the lecture's two key prices: shutdown at £1.50 and break-even at £3 (150 cups). Here \(MC=1.5+q/100\), \(F=£112.50\).
MC = supplyAVCATC

P > min ATC (£3)

Profit. Stay open, and new cafés will want to join (that's L5).

min AVC ≤ P < min ATC

A loss, but stay open in the short run: each cup covers its own cost and chips in towards the rent. Leave when the lease ends.

P < min AVC (£1.50)

Shut now. No cup pays for itself. Your loss is capped at the fixed cost.
\[\text{SR supply}=MC\text{ above min }AVC\qquad\qquad \text{LR supply}=MC\text{ above min }ATC\]

4. Market supply, shifts and elasticity

Add horizontally (just like demand)

Sam: \(q_A=100(P-1.5)\). Leo: \(q_B=100(P-2)\). For \(P\ge2\): \(Q=200P-350\). Below £2 Leo shuts, so there's a kink at £2. Twenty Sams give \(Q=2{,}000(P-1.5)\).

What shifts supply (and what doesn't)

Shifts: input prices (beans, milk, the National Living Wage +6.7% to £12.21 in April 2025), technology, the number of firms, and taxes or regulation. The good's own price only moves you along the curve.

Price elasticity of supply

\(\varepsilon_S=\frac{dQ}{dP}\frac PQ\). On the street at £3: \(2{,}000\times3/3{,}000=2\). Supply is more elastic with spare capacity, low barriers to entry and more time.

Producer surplus

Price minus MC, summed over units: \(\tfrac12\times3{,}000\times£1.50=£2{,}250\)/day. The steeper (more inelastic) supply is, the bigger PS. With vertical supply (Oasis tickets, Edinburgh hotels during the Eras Tour), any rise in demand goes entirely into price.

5. Equilibrium: solve it, then shake it

\[Q_d=9{,}000-2{,}000P,\quad Q_s=2{,}000P-3{,}000\ \Rightarrow\ 12{,}000=4{,}000P\Rightarrow P^*=£3,\ Q^*=3{,}000\]

Price too high (£3.50)

Supply 4,000, demand 2,000: a surplus of 2,000. Unsold pastries and quiet tables push the price down.

Demand ↑ (office opens)

\(Q_d=12{,}000-2{,}000P\) gives \(P=£3.75,\ Q=4{,}500\). Both rise, as a movement along supply.

Cost ↑ 50p (bean shock)

\(Q_s=2{,}000(P-2)\) gives \(P=£3.25,\ Q=2{,}500\). Only 25p of the 50p is passed on, because some customers stop buying.
Pass-through rule of thumb: with linear curves, consumers bear the share \(\frac{\text{slope of }D}{\text{slope of }D+\text{slope of }S}\) (slopes in \(P\)-per-\(Q\) terms). Here the slopes are equal, so it's half. The more inelastic side bears more. The same logic decides who pays a tax in L5.

Quiz: Lecture 4

Lecture 5 · Markets and perfect competition

Profit is a signal, and free entry answers it until it's gone.

In the short run the price absorbs a shock. In the long run the number of firms absorbs it, and the price returns to min ATC with zero economic profit. Any cap or tax that stops trades worth making creates a deadweight loss of \(\tfrac12\times\text{wedge}\times\text{lost quantity}\).
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS2 Q16–17 · PS3 Q1–5, Q11)
R18 Long-run entryR19 Price cap + misallocationR20 TaxR21 Subsidy (not in slides)
Hook: Houston vs New York (1977–2009)
Houston's population roughly doubled and its house prices rose less than threefold. New York grew about 15% and prices rose roughly tenfold at the peak. Houston could build outwards (elastic supply), so demand became homes. New York couldn't (inelastic supply), so demand became price.
Hook: the Dubai chocolate craze
A viral pistachio-and-pastry bar earned big profits, then Lindt, Hotel Chocolat, Lidl and others entered. Entry pushes the price towards cost. Meanwhile pistachio prices rose (€6.65 → €8.96/lb), because growing demand for the bar raised the price of its input. Only uncopyable assets (the original brand) keep profit alive.

1. Four market structures

StructureFirmsProductEntryExample
Perfect competitionMany, smallIdenticalFreeWheat, currencies, a street of cafés
Monopolistic competitionManySlightly differentEasyRestaurants, hairdressers
OligopolyA few bigEitherHigh barriersUK supermarkets, mobile networks
MonopolyOneNo close substitutesBlockedRegional water, a patented drug

Few buyers instead: monopsony (one big employer in a town) or oligopsony (a few supermarkets buying from farmers). The NHS is a big buyer of medicines.

The four assumptions of perfect competition

(1) Many buyers and sellers, so nobody moves the price. (2) An identical product. (3) Perfect information. (4) Free entry and exit. Failures point elsewhere: few sellers means monopoly or oligopoly, and unequal information (used cars) means market failure.

2. The long-run story in six frames

1Demand ↑The office opens, so D shifts right. 2£3 → £3.75In the short run the price takes the shock. 3Sam sells moreUp his MC curve: ~166 cups, ~£119/day profit. 4Profit = signalP is above min ATC, so outsiders notice. 5EntryS shifts right in waves: £3.38, then £3.00. 6Back to £340 cafés, 6,000 cups, zero economic profit.

Flat LR supply

Newcomers copy Sam's cost curves and input prices don't move, so the price is pinned at min ATC (£3). All the extra demand shows up as quantity.

Rising LR supply

As the industry grows, input prices rise (rents, baristas), the best sites are used first, and land is limited. Entry stops at £3.30 with ~5,400 cups.

Firms with different costs

A café with cheap rent (min cost £2.70) keeps 30p a cup, a return to its better site. The marginal firm earns zero economic profit.

In reverse: demand falls to £2.75, below ATC but above AVC. Cafés stay open while losing money (like Britain's pubs: 47,613 → 45,345 in 2019–24) and leave when their leases end, until the price is back at £3.

3. Who gains, and the triangle that nobody gets

\[D:\ P=4.50-\frac{Q}{2000},\qquad S:\ P=1.50+\frac{Q}{2000},\qquad CS=PS=\tfrac12(3000)(1.50)=£2{,}250\]
Live model 5: caps, taxes and deadweight loss on Sam's streetPick a policy and watch the surplus areas move.
CSPStax revenueDWL

The 4-step DWL method

(1) Quantity traded: the short side decides (2,000 under a £2.50 cap). (2) Wedge: demand price minus supply price at that quantity (£3.50 − £2.50 = £1). (3) Lost quantity: efficient minus traded (1,000). (4) \(\tfrac12\times£1\times1{,}000=£500\)/day. Check it against total surplus: £4,500 → £4,000.

DWL grows with the square of the distortion

Cap £2.50 → £500. Cap £2.25 → £1,125. Tax 60p → £180, and tax £1.20 → £720 (4×). A small extra intervention costs disproportionately more.

Berlin's rent cap (2020–21)

Capped rents rose slowly (as intended), but flats offered for rent fell by up to 60% and uncapped rents rose faster. Sitting tenants gained and searchers lost. The court struck it down in April 2021.

UK sugar levy (2018)

Makers reformulated: average sugar fell ~47% while volumes held up. A tax only creates DWL through the trades it stops. Here it stopped few. And if a tax targets a cost the market ignores (a spillover), the trades it stops may not have been worth making.
Who pays a tax doesn't depend on who the law charges. A 60p tax on sellers shifts S up by 60p. Customers pay £3.30 (+30p) and cafés keep £2.70 (−30p). It's split 50/50 here because the slopes are equal. Revenue is \(0.60\times2{,}400=£1{,}440\).

What competition achieves, and its limits

The right quantity (every cup worth more than it costs gets made), at the lowest cost (min ATC), with prices doing the coordinating. Limits: spillovers (cup waste), market power (L6 onwards), and fairness (efficient ≠ fair). Regulators: the CMA (competition), Ofgem (energy price cap), Ofwat (water monopolies).

Quiz: Lecture 5

Lecture 6 · Monopoly and market power

$13.50 → $750. Why not $7,500?

A monopolist faces the whole downward-sloping demand curve, so selling one more unit means cutting the price on every unit: \(MR<P\). It still sets \(MR=MC\), but now \(P>MC\). The markup \(\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac1e\) is limited only by how easily buyers can walk away.
What the problem sets make you do with this lecture (PS3 Q6–10, Q12)
R22 Monopoly Q, P, DWLR23 Markup ruleR24 Capping a monopolistR25 Natural monopoly & break-even cap
Hook: Daraprim, September 2015
Turing Pharmaceuticals raised the price of a 1953 anti-parasitic drug from $13.50 to $750 a pill. Hold two questions until the end of this section. (1) If it can set any price, what stops $7,500? (2) Netflix said its price rise was a mistake. What would we need to know to judge whether $750 was one?

1. Where monopoly comes from: barriers to entry

Legal

Patents and licences (Zantac).

Government-created

A sole right to supply (Royal Mail, historically).

Network economies

More users make it more valuable (Facebook, utilities).

Economies of scale

A huge fixed cost means one firm is cheapest: a natural monopoly (railways).

Behavioural

Threatening a price war to deter entry (L7).

Control of key assets

De Beers and rough diamonds.

Monopoly is a matter of degree and depends on how you define the market. Test it with cross-price elasticity. Pricing power, Buffett's "single most important decision", is measured by the own-price elasticity.

2. Why MR < P (the picture to draw in the exam)

From 1 cup to 2 on \(P=6-Q\)

At Q = 1, P = 5 and TR = 5. To sell Q = 2 the price must fall to 4 for both units, so TR = 8. The second unit brings in +4, but the first unit now earns 1 less. So \(MR=4-1=3\), which is below the £4 price.

In general

\[TR=(a-bQ)Q\ \Rightarrow\ MR=a-2bQ\]
MR has the same intercept, twice the slope. It hits zero halfway to the choke quantity, and that's exactly where \(\varepsilon=1\) (Lecture 2's revenue peak).

3. Profit maximisation in four steps (Sam's kiosk: \(P=6-Q,\ TC=\tfrac12Q^2\))

\[ \begin{aligned} &MR=6-2Q,\quad MC=Q,\quad ATC=\tfrac12Q\\ &\text{1. } MR=MC:\ 6-2Q=Q\Rightarrow Q^*=2\ (200\text{ cups})\\ &\text{2. Price from DEMAND, not MR: } P^*=6-2=£4\quad(\text{MR there is only }2)\\ &\text{3. } ATC(2)=£1\\ &\text{4. } \pi=(P-ATC)\,Q=(4-1)\times2=6\ \Rightarrow\ £600/\text{day} \end{aligned}\]

4. The markup rule (where Lectures 2 and 6 meet)

\[MR=P+Q\frac{dP}{dQ}=P\left(1-\frac1e\right)=MC\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{P=MC\cdot\frac{e}{e-1}}\iff\boxed{L\equiv\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac1e}\]
\(e\)P ÷ MCExample
1.53.0×A medicine with no substitute (£4 to make, £12 to buy)
22.0×The campus hoodie (only one seller of the logo)
41.33×A branded snack with many alternatives
10+≈1.1×Close to perfect competition

Kiosk check: at \(Q=2,P=4\), \(e=1\times4/2=2\), so \(P=2\times MC(2)=2\times2=£4\) ✓. The Lerner index is 0.5.

Markup calculator

A monopolist never prices on the inelastic part of demand. If \(e<1\), then \(MR=P(1-1/e)<0\): selling one fewer unit raises revenue and also saves cost. So it keeps raising the price until \(e>1\). That's the answer to "why not $7,500?": at some point demand becomes elastic enough (substitutes, rationing, regulators, entry) that higher prices lose more than they gain.

5. Is monopoly bad? Count the surplus

Live model 6: the monopoly kiosk, \(P=a-Q,\ MC=Q\)Compare monopoly, competition and price caps. Units: hundreds of cups, £.
CSPSDWL

Monopoly vs competition (a = 6)

Monopoly: 200 cups at £4, CS £200 + PS £600 = £800. Competition: 300 cups at £3, CS £450 + PS £450 = £900. DWL = £100 = \(\tfrac12\times(4-2)\times1\).

Caps

£3.50: Q = 250, profit £562.50, DWL £25. £3 (the competitive price): Q = 300, DWL £0. £2 (too low): the firm makes only 200 (where MC = £2), leaving a shortage of 200 and a DWL back at £100.

Why a cap helps

Under a cap, selling one more unit no longer drags the price down, so MR is flat at the cap. The monopolist behaves like a price taker up to the demand curve.

Costs of monopoly

Deadweight loss · cost inflation (no rival keeping it sharp) · rent-seeking (lobbying and legal fights create nothing).

Benefits of monopoly

Economies of scale (natural monopoly) · patents reward innovation · Schumpeter's creative destruction (the hope of monopoly profit drives innovation, and new innovators then displace old monopolists). So ask whether the benefits outweigh the costs, which depends on how the monopoly arose.

6. Entry kills markups: patent expiry

SellersGeneric price (brand = 100)Why
Brand with patent100No substitutes, so low \(e\)
1 generic61Buyers can switch, so \(e\) rises
2 generics46
4 generics21
6 or more<5P → MC

US FDA, generics entering in 2015–17. With MC = £4: \(e=1.5\) gives £12, \(e=4\) gives £5.33, \(e=20\) gives £4.21.

7. Regulation in practice: RPI − X and natural monopoly

Real price caps

Inflation − X (an efficiency target), first used for BT in 1984. Ofwat, Ofgem and the ORR set the limits. The information problem: the firm knows its MC better than the regulator does. Set the cap too tight and the firm underinvests. Set it too loose and the firm keeps excess profit.

Natural monopoly: one network beats two

F = £1,250/day, MC = £1. One firm serving 2,500 riders: AC = £1.50. Two firms with 1,250 each: AC = £2.00, which wastes £1,250 a day on a duplicate network.
Demand \(P=4-Q/1000\)PriceRidersProfit/dayDWL/dayCatch
Unregulated (MR = MC)£2.501,500+£1,000£1,125Riders who value a ride above £1 are priced out
P = MC (first best)£1.003,000−£1,250£0The loss equals the fixed cost, so it needs a subsidy or a fixed fee
P = AC (second best)£1.502,500£0£125No subsidy needed, but 500 riders are still priced out
🧠 Back to Daraprim: a model answer

Why not $7,500? The firm sets \(MR=MC\), which puts it where \(\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac1e\). The pill is a decades-old, off-patent drug that costs very little to make, so a Lerner index of ~0.99 implies \(e\) only just above 1. At $750 the firm was already near the point where further rises lose enough patients (via hospitals rationing, doctors switching treatments, and insurers refusing to pay) to cut revenue. Above that, demand turns elastic and MR goes negative.

Was it a mistake? Use the Netflix lens: one-period elasticity misses the long run. The drug was off-patent, so the barrier was artificial. The firm moved Daraprim into a closed distribution system and tied up its active-ingredient suppliers to keep generics out. A generic was approved in February 2020. In January 2022 a US court found the scheme anticompetitive, ordered Martin Shkreli to pay $64.6m, and banned him from the pharmaceutical industry for life. That is the "entry + regulators" force in the model: a markup that depends on blocking entry is fragile.

Competition: \(9-Q=Q\Rightarrow Q_c=4.5,\ P_c=£4.50\).
\(DWL=\tfrac12\times(P_m-MC(Q_m))\times(Q_c-Q_m)=\tfrac12\times(6-3)\times1.5=2.25\Rightarrow £225\)/day.

Mark-losing traps

1. Movement vs shift. Only the good's own price moves you along the curve. Everything else shifts it. "Demand rose" (a shift) and "quantity demanded rose" (a movement) are different answers.
2. Adding demand or supply vertically. Always add quantities at each price, horizontally. Then hunt for kinks at each choke or shutdown price.
3. Slope ≠ elasticity. A straight line has a constant slope but \(\varepsilon\) varies from 0 to ∞ along it. Only the vertical and horizontal extremes can be read off the picture.
4. Comparing price with AC instead of MC. The overtime unit: AC is £42 but MC is £58, so don't sell it at £50.
5. Letting sunk costs into a decision. £1bn spent is irrelevant. Compare future costs with future benefits only.
6. Reading the monopoly price off MR. MR = MC gives the quantity. The price comes from the demand curve at that quantity.
7. Shutdown vs exit. Short run: compare P with min AVC (fixed costs are paid regardless). Long run: compare P with min ATC.
8. Zero economic profit = "earning nothing". No. It means earning exactly your best alternative (normal profit).
9. "The tax falls on whoever the law charges." No. Incidence depends on relative elasticities. The more inelastic side pays more.
10. A cap always helps buyers. Only down to the competitive price. Below it, a shortage appears and the DWL comes back.
11. Units. The pizza stall's Q is in '000/day and the kiosk's Q is in hundreds. A profit of "6" is £600. State your units.
12. Short run vs long run elasticity. Netflix's 0.05 was one quarter. Elasticities of demand and supply both grow with time.

Built from Problem Sets 1–3

The playbook: every question type, as a recipe

The problem sets reuse the same 27 moves. Each recipe gives the steps, a worked example from the sheets, and the wrong option the examiner plants. Learn the recipes and the questions become routine.

L1

R1 · Find the optimal bundle (Cobb-Douglas)

PS1 Q1, Q11(a)(b)
  1. Write the marginal utilities: \(MU_1=\partial u/\partial x_1\) and \(MU_2=\partial u/\partial x_2\).
  2. Set the tangency condition: \(MRS=\dfrac{MU_1}{MU_2}=\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}\).
  3. Solve it for \(x_2\) in terms of \(x_1\), then substitute into \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2=M\).
  4. Shortcut once you trust it: for \(u=x_1^{a}x_2^{b}\), good 1 gets the budget share \(\frac{a}{a+b}\), so \(x_1^*=\frac{a}{a+b}\frac{M}{p_1}\). With \(a+b=1\) this is \(x_1^*=\alpha M/p_1\).

The intuition the sheet asks for: \(MU_1/MU_2\) is the rate at which he is willing to swap good 2 for good 1. \(p_1/p_2\) is the rate at which the market lets him. If they differ, moving £1 from one good to the other raises utility, so he stops only when they are equal.

Worked: PS1 Q11, \(u=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\), \(p_1=p_2=£1\), \(M=£9\) \(MU_1=\tfrac13x_1^{-2/3}x_2^{2/3}\), \(MU_2=\tfrac23x_1^{1/3}x_2^{-1/3}\), so \(\frac{MU_1}{MU_2}=\frac{x_2}{2x_1}=\frac{p_1}{p_2}=1\Rightarrow x_2=2x_1\).
The budget \(x_1+x_2=9\) gives \(3x_1=9\), so \(x_1^*=3,\ x_2^*=6\). Spending is £3 and £6: shares of \(\tfrac13\) and \(\tfrac23\), equal to the exponents.
Planted wrong answers (PS1 Q1): forgetting \(\alpha\) (gives \(M/p_1\)), dividing by the wrong price, or halving the answer.
L1

R2 · Read every elasticity off a demand function with logs

PS1 Q11(c)(d)(e), Q12(d)
  1. Take logs of the demand function. For \(x_1=\frac{\alpha M}{p_1}\): \(\ln x_1=\ln\alpha+\ln M-\ln p_1\).
  2. The coefficient on each log is the elasticity: own price \(-1\Rightarrow\varepsilon=1\), income \(+1\Rightarrow\varepsilon_M=1\), no \(\ln p_2\) term \(\Rightarrow\varepsilon_X=0\).
  3. In general, \(x=A\,p^{-k}M^{m}p_2^{c}\) has \(\varepsilon=k\), \(\varepsilon_M=m\) and \(\varepsilon_X=c\), the same at every price.
  4. Interpret: \(\varepsilon=1\) means spending is constant, so a seller's revenue from this buyer doesn't change with price. \(\varepsilon_M=1\) means a normal good but not a luxury (the budget share stays fixed).
Worked: PS1 Q11(d)(e) \(p_1\) doubles to £2: \(x_1=9/(3\times2)=1.5\) and \(x_2\) stays at 6. That is a movement along good 1's demand curve. Good 2's curve doesn't move, because \(\varepsilon_X=0\). Spending on good 1 is still £3.
\(M\) rises to £18: \((6,12)\), a shift right of both demand curves (income isn't on either axis).
L2/L4

R3 · Add individual demand (or supply) curves and handle the kinks

PS1 Q4 · PS2 Q12
  1. Find each person's choke price (demand reaches 0) or each firm's threshold price (supply starts).
  2. At the price asked about, list who is still in the market. Never let a quantity go negative.
  3. Add the quantities horizontally at that price. For the whole function, write one formula per price band and check that the pieces join at each kink.
Worked PS1 Q4: \(x_A=10-p\) (0 above £10) and \(x_B=6-p/2\). At \(p=11\) only B buys: \(6-5.5=\mathbf{0.5}\).
PS2 Q12: \(q_A=10(P-2)\) and \(q_B=5(P-4)\). At £6, \(40+10=\mathbf{50}\). The kink is at £4, where B opens.
Planted wrong answer: \(-0.5\), from adding A's formula past her choke price.
L2/L4

R4 · Movement or shift? A two-question classifier

PS1 Q2, Q3 · PS2 Q13 · PS1 Q11(d)(e)
  1. Did the good's own price change? Yes → movement along the curve. Stop there.
  2. No → the curve shifts. Work out the direction:
EventCurveDirection
A substitute gets cheaper (pears ↓ for apples)DemandLeft
A complement gets cheaper (ink ↓ for printers)DemandRight
Income ↑, normal goodDemandRight
Income ↑, inferior good (noodles)DemandLeft
An input gets cheaper (milk ↓)SupplyRight
Rents or wages ↑, or a taxSupplyLeft
More firms, better technologySupplyRight
More customers (office block)Demand (not supply!)Right
Planted wrong answer: "No change, because the price hasn't changed." Demand changed even though the price didn't.
L2

R5 · Compute an elasticity, and know where the formula is valid

PS1 Q5, Q6, Q12(a)–(d)
  1. From % changes: \(\varepsilon=\dfrac{|\%\Delta Q|}{|\%\Delta P|}\). A price rise from £10 to £12 is +20%, and a 15% fall in quantity gives \(\varepsilon=0.75\).
  2. Point formula on a line \(Q=a-bP\): \(\varepsilon=\dfrac{bP}{a-bP}\). Unit elastic at \(P=\frac a{2b}\).
  3. Validity: only where \(Q>0\), i.e. below the choke price \(a/b\). At \(P=30\) on \(100-5P\), the "quantity" is −50, so \(\varepsilon\) is undefined.
  4. Comparing two straight lines: you can't without knowing the prices, because elasticity varies along each line. At the same price, compare \(\frac{b_1P}{a_1-b_1P}\) with \(\frac{b_2P}{a_2-b_2P}\). Slopes alone don't decide it.
  5. Constant-elasticity curve \(Q=Ap^{-k}\): \(\varepsilon=k\) everywhere, so you can compare without prices.
  6. Cross-price: the sign tells you the relationship. \(-6\%/+20\%=-0.3\) means complements.
Worked: PS1 Q12(b)(c) \(D_1=100-5p\): \(\varepsilon(2)=10/90\approx0.11\), \(\varepsilon(10)=1\), \(\varepsilon(15)=3\).
Against \(D_2=200-3p\) at the same \(p<20\): \(5(200-3p)>3(100-5p)\), i.e. \(1000-15p>300-15p\), which is always true. So good 1 is more elastic at any common price.
L2

R6 · Revenue after a price change: exact vs approximate, and the advice

PS1 Q7, Q8, Q9, Q12(e), Q13
  1. Exact: compute \(Q\) at both prices, then \(\%\Delta TR=\frac{P_1Q_1-P_0Q_0}{P_0Q_0}\).
  2. From an elasticity alone: \(\frac{TR_1}{TR_0}=(1+\%\Delta P)(1-\varepsilon\,\%\Delta P)\). With \(\varepsilon=0.4\) and +10%: \(1.10\times0.96=1.056\), so +5.6%.
  3. Linear approximation: \(\%\Delta TR\approx(1-\varepsilon)\,\%\Delta P\). It is only exact for small changes, because \(\varepsilon\) itself changes as you move along the curve.
  4. Advice: \(\varepsilon<1\) → raise the price. \(\varepsilon>1\) → cut it. \(\varepsilon=1\) → leave it (revenue peak). \(\varepsilon<1\) and \(MC>0\) → raise, because revenue rises and cost falls, so profit rises for sure. \(\varepsilon\) small now but big later → be careful (Netflix).
Worked: PS1 Q13, \(Q=120-4P\) \(\varepsilon=4P/Q\): 0.5 at £10 and 2 at £20. Revenue peaks at £15 (Q = 60, TR = £900).
£10 → £11: TR 800 → 836, +4.5% (the approximation says +5%). Raise, because demand is inelastic.
£20 → £18: TR 800 → 864, +8% (the approximation says +10%). Cut, because demand is elastic.
PS1 Q12(e): \(100-5p\) at £15 → £16.50 gives TR 375 → 288.75, −23% against an approximation of −20%.
L2

R7 · Consumer surplus

PS1 Q10 · PS2 Q17(c) · PS3 Q11, Q12
  1. Write demand in inverse form \(P=A-bQ\). \(A\) is the choke price (the top of the triangle).
  2. Quantity at the price: \(Q=(A-P)/b\).
  3. \(CS=\tfrac12\,Q\,(A-P)\). If a cap or tax makes the shape a trapezium, split it into a rectangle plus a triangle.
Worked: PS1 Q10, \(P=20-Q\) at £8\(Q=12\), so \(CS=\tfrac12\times12\times(20-8)=\mathbf{72}\).
Planted wrong answers: using the quantity-axis intercept as the height, or forgetting the ½.
L2

R8 · Price discrimination: who pays more, and what stops arbitrage

PS1 Q13(e)
  1. Rank the groups by elasticity. Charge more to the inelastic group (business travellers, \(\varepsilon=0.5\)) and less to the elastic one (leisure, \(\varepsilon=2\)).
  2. Why it beats a single price: one fare is too low for the inelastic group and too high for the elastic group, so it leaves money on the table on both sides.
  3. Three conditions: market power, a way to tell the groups apart (or let them self-select), and no arbitrage.
  4. Name the fences: advance purchase, non-refundable or non-changeable tickets, Saturday-night stay, named tickets, student ID, versioning.
L3

R9 · Opportunity cost and sunk cost decisions

PS2 Q1, Q2
  1. The cost of using something you own is its best alternative use. Amira's van costs £60 a day (the rent she gives up), not £0 and not the £30,000 she paid.
  2. For a decision, compare only future costs and benefits. Anything already spent and unrecoverable is sunk, so delete it from the comparison.
Worked: PS2 Q2£2m spent so far. Finishing costs £1.5m more and brings £1.2m, so the marginal decision is −£0.3m: stop.
Planted wrong answer: "Stop because the total cost of £3.5m exceeds £1.2m." That's the right decision for the wrong reason (it counts the sunk £2m), and it would score zero in a written answer.
L3

R10 · Marginal cost from a production table

PS2 Q3
  1. \(MP=\Delta Q\) from one more worker.
  2. \(MC=\dfrac{w}{MP}\): the worker's wage spread over the extra units they add.
Worked4 workers make 120 and 5 make 140, so MP = 20. With \(w=£40\), \(MC=40/20=\mathbf{£2}\).
Planted wrong answers: \(w/Q\) (40/140 or 40/120). That's an average, not a marginal.
L3

R11 · All the cost curves from TC, and their minimum points

PS2 Q4, Q18(a)
  1. Split \(TC\) into \(F\) (the constant) and \(VC(q)\).
  2. \(AVC=VC/q\), \(ATC=TC/q\), \(MC=TC'(q)\).
  3. Min AVC: \(\frac{d\,AVC}{dq}=0\). Min ATC: \(\frac{d\,ATC}{dq}=0\), or equivalently \(MC=ATC\).
  4. Check that \(MC\) equals the average at its minimum. Explain why: a marginal unit below the average pulls it down, and one above pushes it up.
  5. Quadratic shortcut, \(TC=F+cq+dq^2\): \(q^*=\sqrt{F/d}\), \(ATC_{\min}=c+2\sqrt{Fd}\).
  6. Cubic: you'll get a cubic in \(q\). Try small integers, since the sheet usually hints at the root.
Worked: PS2 Q4 and Q18(a) \(TC=200+2q+0.5q^2\): \(ATC=200/q+2+0.5q\), so \(-200/q^2+0.5=0\Rightarrow q=20\), \(ATC=\mathbf{£22}=MC(20)\).
Kiosk \(TC=6.4+2.4q-0.4q^2+0.1q^3\): \(AVC=2.4-0.4q+0.1q^2\) is lowest at \(q=2\) (£2.00). For \(ATC\), set the slope to zero and multiply by \(5q^2\): \(q^3-2q^2-32=0\), so \(q=4\) and \(ATC=£4.00=MC(4)\).
Planted wrong answer: forgetting the fixed part of average cost (PS2 Q4 option B).
L3

R12 · The cost-minimising input mix

PS2 Q5
  1. Set \(\dfrac{MPL}{MPK}=\dfrac wr\). For \(y=\sqrt{KL}\) (or any \(K^aL^a\)), \(\frac{MPL}{MPK}=\frac KL\), so \(K=\frac wr L\).
  2. Substitute into the production function and solve for \(L\), then \(K\).
  3. Cost \(=wL+rK\). Check it against the shortcut \(C=2y\sqrt{rw}\).
  4. General Cobb-Douglas \(y=K^aL^b\): \(\dfrac{wL}{rK}=\dfrac ba\), so spending splits in the ratio of the exponents.
Worked: PS2 Q5, \(w=9,\ r=4,\ y=60\)\(K=2.25L\), so \(60=\sqrt{2.25L^2}=1.5L\Rightarrow L^*=40,\ K^*=90\). Cost \(=9(40)+4(90)=\mathbf{£720}=2\times60\times\sqrt{36}\).
Planted wrong answer: swapping the inputs, i.e. using more of the dearer one (£970).
L3

R13 · Returns to scale → the shape of LATC

PS2 Q6
  1. For \(K^aL^b\), compute \(a+b\). Doubling the inputs multiplies output by \(2^{a+b}\).
  2. \(a+b>1\): increasing returns, LATC falls. \(=1\): constant, LATC flat. \(<1\): decreasing, LATC rises.
  3. Why: costs double while output more than, exactly, or less than doubles.
Worked\(K^{0.4}L^{0.5}\): \(2^{0.9}\approx1.87<2\), so decreasing returns and LATC slopes up.
Don't confuse this with diminishing marginal returns (one input varies, the others are fixed, in the short run).
L4

R14 · Accounting vs economic profit

PS2 Q7
  1. Accounting = revenue − explicit bills.
  2. Economic = accounting − opportunity costs (the owner's forgone salary, rent and return on capital).
  3. Economic < 0 means she'd do better elsewhere, even if the accountant reports a profit.
Worked: PS2 Q7£90k − £70k = £20k accounting. Minus £25k forgone salary = −£5k economic. The £25k is her normal profit.
L4

R15 · Price taker: output and profit

PS2 Q8, Q9, Q18(b) · PS3 Q2
  1. \(MR=P\) (every extra unit adds exactly the price).
  2. Set \(P=MC(q)\) and solve. If \(MC\) is quadratic, use the formula and keep the root on the rising part of MC.
  3. Check that \(P\ge AVC(q)\). If not, \(q=0\).
  4. Profit \(=Pq-TC(q)\). Don't report revenue by mistake.
Worked PS3 Q2: \(200=40+4Q\Rightarrow Q=\mathbf{40}\) tonnes.
PS2 Q9: \(TC=50+2q+q^2\), \(P=22\): \(22=2+2q\Rightarrow q=10\). Profit \(=220-170=\mathbf{£50}\).
Kiosk at £2.70: \(2.7=2.4-0.8q+0.3q^2\Rightarrow3q^2-8q-3=0\Rightarrow(3q+1)(q-3)=0\Rightarrow q=3\).
L4

R16 · Shut down, stay open, or exit (the avoidable-cost rule)

PS2 Q10, Q11, Q18(b)(c)
  1. Find min AVC (the shutdown price) and min ATC (the exit/break-even price).
  2. \(P>\min ATC\): profit, stay. \(\min AVC\le P<\min ATC\): loss, but stay open in the short run and exit when the lease ends. \(P<\min AVC\): close now.
  3. Prove it with numbers: loss if open \(=(P-ATC)\,q\), loss if closed \(=\) unavoidable fixed cost.
  4. The general rule (the Q18(c) essay): the shutdown price is the minimum average of the costs that are still avoidable. If a lease lets the rent stop while closed, the rent becomes avoidable, so the relevant price jumps from min AVC to min ATC.
  5. Supply curves: SR = MC above min AVC. LR (one firm) = MC above min ATC.
Worked: PS2 Q18(b) kiosk at £2.70q = 3. Revenue 8.1, VC 6.3, TC 12.7. Open: −£4,600. Closed: −£6,400 (rent). So stay open: the takings cover VC and contribute £1,800 to the rent. At £1.80 (below £2.00), close. Under a "no rent while closed" lease, close at £2.70 (lose £0 instead of £4,600).
Planted wrong answer: "Raise its price to £6." A price taker can't.
L4

R17 · Equilibrium, a stuck price, and combined shifts

PS2 Q14, Q15, Q17(a)(b)
  1. Set \(Q_d=Q_s\), solve for \(P\), then substitute back into both equations as a check.
  2. To draw it: the price-axis intercepts are where \(Q=0\) (demand's choke, supply's threshold). Pick one more point on each line.
  3. Price stuck at \(\bar P\): compute \(Q_d(\bar P)\) and \(Q_s(\bar P)\). The difference is the shortage or surplus. Say which way the price is pushed and why.
  4. Two shifts at once: solve the new equilibrium. Then decompose: solve with only the demand shift, then with only the supply shift, to say which moved the price more.
  5. D↑ with S↓: the price rises for sure, and the quantity depends on which shift is bigger.
  6. Vertical supply (fixed seats): all of a demand shift goes into the price.
Worked: PS2 Q17, bubble tea \(1200-100P=200P-600\Rightarrow P=£6,\ Q=600\). At £5: demand 700, supply 400, a shortage of 300.
New \(Q_d=1800-100P\), \(Q_s=200(P-4.5)\): \(2700=300P\Rightarrow P=£9,\ Q=900\).
Demand shift alone → £8. Supply shift alone → £7. So the demand shift moved the price more.
Long run: entry pushes the price back down towards the (now higher) min ATC.
Planted wrong answer (PS2 Q14): the right price with an arithmetic slip in Q. Always check both curves.
L5

R18 · Long-run entry: where does the price end up?

PS2 Q16 · PS3 Q1, Q3
  1. The short run after demand ↑: the price rises and existing firms make supernormal profit.
  2. Free entry shifts supply right until profit = 0.
  3. Constant costs (entrants copy the incumbents and input prices don't move): the price returns to the same min ATC with more firms. LR supply is flat.
  4. Increasing costs (land, labour and best sites get dearer as the industry grows): a higher price and a higher quantity. LR supply slopes up (PS3 Q3 → C).
L5

R19 · A price cap: shortage, surpluses, DWL, and misallocation

PS2 Q17(c) · PS3 Q4, Q11(b)(c)
  1. Free market: \(P^*,Q^*\).
  2. At the cap \(c<P^*\): \(Q_s(c)\) is traded (the short side). The shortage is \(Q_d(c)-Q_s(c)\).
  3. Wedge \(=P_d(Q_s)-c\), where \(P_d\) is the demand price at the traded quantity.
  4. \(DWL=\tfrac12\times\text{wedge}\times(Q^*-Q_s)\).
  5. \(CS\) = a rectangle \(Q_s\,(P_d-c)\) plus a triangle \(\tfrac12Q_s(A-P_d)\). \(PS=\tfrac12Q_s(c-\text{supply intercept})\). Check that total surplus falls by exactly the DWL.
  6. Misallocation: the DWL triangle assumes the units go to the buyers who value them most. If they're allocated by queue or luck, some go to low-value buyers. With linear demand, the average willingness to pay of everyone who wants a unit at the cap is \(\frac{A+c}{2}\), so the expected \(CS=Q_s\left(\frac{A+c}{2}-c\right)\), which is lower. Queueing time is a further loss on top.
Worked: PS3 Q4, \(P=120-Q\), \(P=20+Q\), cap £50\(Q^*=50,\ P^*=70\). At £50 supply is 30 and demand is 70. \(P_d(30)=90\), so the wedge is 40. \(DWL=\tfrac12\times40\times20=\mathbf{400}\) (£ thousand). Answer D.
L5

R20 · A per-unit tax: prices, revenue, DWL and incidence

PS3 Q5
  1. Shift supply up by \(t\): \(P=B+Q+t\). It makes no difference who the law charges.
  2. Solve with demand to get \(Q_t\) and the buyers' price \(P_c\). Sellers keep \(P_s=P_c-t\).
  3. Revenue \(=tQ_t\). \(DWL=\tfrac12\,t\,(Q^*-Q_t)\).
  4. Incidence: the more inelastic side bears more. With equal slopes it's 50/50.
  5. DWL grows with \(t^2\): double the tax, quadruple the loss.
Worked: PS3 Q5, \(P=90-Q\), \(P=10+Q\), \(t=8\)\(Q^*=40\). With the tax: \(90-Q=18+Q\Rightarrow Q_t=36\). \(DWL=\tfrac12\times8\times4=\mathbf{16}\). Buyers pay £54 and sellers keep £46. Revenue = 288. Answer B.
L5

R21 · A per-unit subsidy (on PS3 but not in the lectures)

PS3 Q11(e) [Level 6]
  1. A subsidy \(s\) lowers the cost of supplying each unit, so supply shifts down by \(s\): \(P=B-s+bQ\).
  2. Buyers pay \(P_c\) and sellers receive \(P_c+s\). The quantity rises above the efficient \(Q^*\).
  3. Cost to the government \(=s\times Q_{sub}\).
  4. \(DWL=\tfrac12\,s\,(Q_{sub}-Q^*)\). Units past \(Q^*\) cost more to make than buyers value them (over-production).
  5. To hit a target buyer price \(\bar P\): \(Q=Q_d(\bar P)\), then choose \(s\) so that the subsidised supply curve passes through \((Q,\bar P)\).
  6. Compared with a cap at the same \(\bar P\): no shortage and many more units, but it costs taxpayers money and still creates a DWL.
L6

R22 · Monopoly: Q, P, profit, CS and DWL

PS3 Q6, Q8, Q12(a)(c)
  1. \(P=A-bQ\Rightarrow MR=A-2bQ\) (twice the slope).
  2. \(MR=MC\Rightarrow Q_m\). The price comes from demand: \(P_m=A-bQ_m\).
  3. Profit \(=(P_m-AC)\,Q_m=(P_m-c)\,Q_m-F\).
  4. Competitive benchmark: \(P=MC\Rightarrow Q_c\).
  5. \(DWL=\tfrac12\,(P_m-MC(Q_m))\,(Q_c-Q_m)\). \(CS_m=\tfrac12Q_m(A-P_m)\).
  6. Shortcut (linear demand, constant \(c\)): \(Q_m=\frac{Q_c}{2}\), \(P_m=\frac{A+c}{2}\), \(DWL=\frac{(A-c)^2}{8b}\).
Worked PS3 Q6 ferry: \(80-4Q=20\Rightarrow Q=15,\ P=\mathbf{£50}\) (D).
PS3 Q8: \(100-2Q=20\Rightarrow Q_m=40,\ P_m=60\). \(Q_c=80\). \(DWL=\tfrac12(40)(40)=\mathbf{800}\) (C).
Planted wrong answer: reading the price off MR (£35 on the ferry), or charging MC (£20).
L6

R23 · Elasticity at the optimum and the markup rule

PS3 Q7, Q12(b)
  1. At \((Q_m,P_m)\) on \(P=A-bQ\): \(\varepsilon=-\frac{dQ}{dP}\frac PQ=\frac1b\cdot\frac{P_m}{Q_m}\).
  2. Verify: \(P=MC\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}\). Equivalently \(\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac1\varepsilon\).
  3. A rival makes demand more elastic, so \(\varepsilon\) rises and the markup shrinks towards 1.
  4. Being told \(\varepsilon<1\) means MR < 0: raise the price, because revenue rises and costs fall.
L6

R24 · Capping a monopolist's price

PS3 Q9, Q12(d)
  1. Under a cap \(c\), MR is flat at \(c\) up to the demand curve, so the monopolist acts like a price taker.
  2. If \(MC\le c\) at \(Q_d(c)\), it sells \(Q_d(c)\) (constant MC: always true for \(c\ge MC\)).
  3. \(DWL=\tfrac12\,(c-MC)\,(Q_c-Q_d(c))\). Profit \(=(c-MC)\,Q-F\).
  4. A cap at the competitive price removes the DWL. A cap below it (with rising MC) creates a shortage and brings the DWL back.
Worked: PS3 Q9, cap £40 on \(P=100-Q\), \(MC=20\)Q = 60. \(DWL=\tfrac12(40-20)(80-60)=\mathbf{200}\). Answer B.
L6

R25 · Natural monopoly, the break-even cap, and the FOC/SOC

PS3 Q10, Q12(f)
  1. \(P=MC\) with a fixed cost \(F\) means profit \(=-F\). The firm needs a subsidy or a fixed fee.
  2. Lowest break-even cap: solve \((c-MC)\cdot Q_d(c)=F\), a quadratic in \(c\), and take the lower root. This is \(P=AC\) on the demand curve.
  3. FOC/SOC: \(\pi(Q)=P(Q)Q-cQ-F\). \(\pi'(Q)=0\) gives \(Q^*\). \(\pi''(Q)=-2b<0\), so it's a maximum.
  4. \(F\) doesn't change \(Q^*\) or \(P^*\). It only decides whether entering (or investing) is worthwhile.
All

R26 · Diagram checklist (the sheets say "label every axis")

PS2 Q17, Q18 · PS3 Q11, Q12
  1. P on the vertical axis, Q on the horizontal, both with units ("£ per cup", "cups per week").
  2. Compute and mark the intercepts: the choke price, the supply threshold, and where demand hits the Q axis.
  3. Label every curve (D, S, MR, MC, ATC). Use solid for "before" and dashed for "after".
  4. Mark equilibria with their numbers and draw dashed lines to both axes.
  5. Shade and label CS, PS, tax revenue and DWL. State their values beside the figure.
  6. For monopoly, always draw MR with twice the slope, starting from the same intercept.
All

R27 · The 150-word consultant memo or short essay

PS2 Q17(c), Q18(c) · PS3 Q11(d), Q12(e)
  1. Recommendation in the first sentence. Adopt, reject, or "do X instead".
  2. Mechanism in one line: the model that drives it (a cap below equilibrium → shortage; less elastic demand → bigger markup).
  3. Your numbers from the earlier parts: shortage, DWL, profit.
  4. Who gains and who loses. Insiders vs outsiders, firm vs consumers vs taxpayers.
  5. Short run vs long run. Elasticity grows with time, entry happens, investment responds.
  6. A better alternative or combination, and its trade-off.
  7. One real case from the lectures: Berlin, Netflix, Oasis, Daraprim, patents and generics, pubs.

PS3: full worked solutions

Try each question first, then open the solution. Money is in £ thousand where the sheet says so. Every answer below was checked by recomputing it.

Part A

Q1 · Food-festival stalls in the long runB. Positive profit plus free entry with identical costs: entry shifts supply right until the price falls to min ATC and economic profit is zero. A is wrong because each stall takes the price, but the market price still falls as supply grows. R18
Q2 · Wheat farmer, \(MC=40+4Q\), \(P=200\)A, 40 tonnes. \(200=40+4Q\Rightarrow Q=40\). R15
Q3 · Cocoa desserts with rising input pricesC, a higher price and a higher quantity. Entry raises output, but land and labour get dearer as the industry grows, so every grower's min ATC rises. LR supply slopes up. R18
Q4 · Parking-permit cap at £50D, 400. \(120-Q=20+Q\Rightarrow Q^*=50,\ P^*=70\). At £50: \(Q_s=30\) and \(Q_d=70\). \(P_d(30)=90\), so the wedge is \(90-50=40\). \(DWL=\tfrac12\times40\times(50-30)=400\) (£ thousand). R19
Q5 · £8 soft-drink levyB, 16. \(Q^*=40\). With the levy, \(90-Q=18+Q\Rightarrow Q=36\). \(DWL=\tfrac12\times8\times4=16\). (288 is the tax revenue, a trap.) R20
Q6 · Island ferry, \(P=80-2Q\), \(MC=20\)D, £50. \(MR=80-4Q=20\Rightarrow Q=15\), so \(P=80-30=50\). £35 reads the price off MR, and £65 is a slip. R22
Q7 · Monopolist told \(\varepsilon=0.8\)A. With \(\varepsilon<1\), \(MR=P(1-1/\varepsilon)<0\). A higher price raises revenue and lowers costs. B is backwards: a monopolist never operates where demand is inelastic. R23
Q8 · Monopoly DWL, \(P=100-Q\), \(MC=20\)C, 800. \(Q_m=40,\ P_m=60\), \(Q_c=80\). \(DWL=\tfrac12(60-20)(80-40)=800\). Shortcut: \((A-c)^2/8b=6400/8\). R22
Q9 · Cap of £40 on that monopolistB, 60 units and 200. MR is flat at £40 up to demand, and \(MC=20<40\), so it sells \(Q_d(40)=60\). \(DWL=\tfrac12(40-20)(80-60)=200\). R24
Q10 · Water company forced to \(P=MC\)A, −£3,000. Price = MC earns nothing on each unit above variable cost, so the firm loses its whole fixed cost. The 1,500 units are a distractor. R25

Part B · Q11 Capping rents in a student city

\(P=200-2Q\), \(P=20+2Q\). P in £/week, Q in thousand rooms, so areas are £ thousand per week.

(a) Equilibrium\(200-2Q=20+2Q\Rightarrow Q^*=45\) thousand rooms, \(P^*=£110\). Diagram: demand from (0, 200) to (100, 0), supply from (0, 20) through (45, 110).
(b) The £80 capDemand: \(80=200-2Q\Rightarrow Q_d=60\). Supply: \(80=20+2Q\Rightarrow Q_s=30\). 30 thousand rented (the short side) and a shortage of 30 thousand.
(c) Surplus before and after, DWL, and why queueing makes it worse Before: \(CS=\tfrac12(45)(200-110)=2{,}025\), \(PS=\tfrac12(45)(110-20)=2{,}025\), total 4,050.
After (efficient allocation): \(P_d(30)=140\). \(CS=30(140-80)+\tfrac12(30)(200-140)=1{,}800+900=2{,}700\). \(PS=\tfrac12(30)(80-20)=900\). Total 3,600.
DWL \(=\tfrac12(140-80)(45-30)=450\) = 4,050 − 3,600 ✓ (£450k a week).
Random allocation: 60k students want a room at £80, with valuations spread evenly from £80 to £200 (mean £140). If the 30k rooms go by luck, the expected \(CS=30\times(140-80)=1{,}800\), so a further 900 is lost, plus the time spent queueing and searching. The triangle is the minimum loss.
(d) Consultant recommendation (model answer, ~150 words) Do not adopt the £80 cap on its own. At £80 landlords offer 30,000 rooms instead of 45,000, so 15,000 students who would pay the market rent go without, and total surplus falls by at least £450k a week. It falls by up to £900k more if rooms go to whoever queues first rather than whoever values them most. Students who keep a room gain (CS rises from £2,025k to £2,700k), while landlords lose £1,125k and flat-hunters lose most. The damage grows over time: long-run supply is more elastic, so landlords sell, convert or stop letting, as in Berlin, where listings fell by up to 60%. A better policy makes supply more elastic through faster planning permission and purpose-built student housing, which lowers rents without a shortage. If help is needed now, target support at low-income students rather than capping every rent.
(e) [Level 6] A subsidy to reach £80 Students pay £80, so \(Q_d=60\). Subsidised supply is \(P=20-s+2Q\). Passing it through (60, 80) gives \(80=20-s+120\Rightarrow s=£60\) per room per week. Landlords receive £140.
Cost to the council \(=60\times60=3{,}600\) (£3.6m a week).
\(DWL=\tfrac12\,s\,(60-45)=\tfrac12(60)(15)=450\). Rooms 45 to 60 cost up to £140 to supply but students value them at only £80 to £110.
Against the cap: 60k rooms vs 30k, with no shortage, but a £3.6m weekly bill and a DWL of the same size (450) from over-supply instead of under-supply. R21

Part B · Q12 Pricing a patented medicine

\(P=240-2Q\), \(MC=40\), \(F=1{,}800\). P in £/pack, Q in thousand packs, money in £ thousand.

(a) Monopoly optimum\(MR=240-4Q=40\Rightarrow Q_m=50\), \(P_m=240-100=£140\). Profit \(=(140-40)\times50-1{,}800=5{,}000-1{,}800=\mathbf{3{,}200}\) (£3.2m). The diagram: D from 240, MR from 240 with twice the slope hitting 0 at Q = 60, MC flat at 40.
(b) Elasticity and the markup rule\(Q=120-P/2\), so \(\varepsilon=\frac12\cdot\frac{140}{50}=1.4\). Check: \(MC\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}=40\times\frac{1.4}{0.4}=140\) ✓. A rival makes demand more elastic, so \(\varepsilon\) rises, \(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}\) falls towards 1, and the markup shrinks.
(c) After the patent expiresCompetition: \(P=MC=40\), \(Q_c=100\).
\(CS_m=\tfrac12(50)(240-140)=2{,}500\). \(CS_c=\tfrac12(100)(240-40)=10{,}000\).
\(DWL=\tfrac12(140-40)(100-50)=\mathbf{2{,}500}\). (Of the extra 7,500 of CS, 5,000 is the transfer of monopoly profit and 2,500 is the recovered DWL.)
(d) A £90 cap \(Q=Q_d(90)=75\) (MC = 40 < 90). Profit \(=(90-40)(75)-1{,}800=\mathbf{1{,}950}\). \(CS=\tfrac12(75)(240-90)=5{,}625\). \(DWL=\tfrac12(90-40)(100-75)=625\).
At \(P=MC=40\), profit \(=-1{,}800\): the firm never recovers its development cost. So the £90 cap leaves it better off by 3,750. Implication: if regulators routinely push prices to MC once a drug exists, firms anticipate it and won't sink the fixed R&D cost in the first place. The cap has to stay above the break-even level (see f) to protect innovation.
(e) Strategy memo before and after the rival (model answer) Before launch, hold £140: with \(\varepsilon=1.4\) it already maximises profit, and a higher price would cut profit and invite a regulatory cap, as Daraprim did. Use the two years to make demand less elastic later: build switching costs through clinician training, hospital and NHS supply contracts, and device familiarity. Consider a cheaper second version to occupy the price-sensitive segment before the rival can. After launch, demand facing you becomes more elastic, so the profit-maximising markup \(P=MC\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}\) falls. Plan to cut the price towards the rival's and compete on reliability and brand rather than defend £140. Price-discriminate where demand stays inelastic (by channel or country) while preventing resale. Ignore the £1.8m development cost when setting price: it is sunk. Expect the margin to keep falling as more entrants arrive, as with generics.
(f) [Level 6] FOC/SOC and the lowest break-even cap (i) \(\pi(Q)=(240-2Q)Q-40Q-1{,}800=200Q-2Q^2-1{,}800\). FOC: \(\pi'(Q)=200-4Q=0\Rightarrow Q=50\) ✓. SOC: \(\pi''(Q)=-4<0\), so it's a maximum.
(ii) Under a cap \(c\) between 40 and 140 the firm sells \(Q=(240-c)/2\). Break even: \((c-40)\frac{240-c}{2}=1{,}800\Rightarrow c^2-280c+13{,}200=0\Rightarrow c=\frac{280\pm160}{2}\in\{60,220\}\).
The lowest break-even cap is £60, with \(Q=90\) and \(DWL=\tfrac12(60-40)(100-90)=\mathbf{100}\). That is \(P=AC\): \(AC(90)=40+1{,}800/90=60\) ✓. R25
